title: K-H-L
hookLine: kahal, kehillah: an assembly, a community

lines: A BOOK WITH A TITLE, NOT A NAME.
cards: There's a book in the Bible whose author doesn't give a name, just a title: Kohelet. It opens with a man looking hard at life and calling all of it vapor, breath, here and gone.

English Bibles call the book Ecclesiastes, and the speaker the Preacher. But Kohelet comes from a root that means to gather a crowd: something like the Gatherer, or the one who speaks to the assembly.
A book this lonely-sounding is named for a crowd.

teach.b: K-H-L. Kuf, hey, lamed. Kahal: an assembly, a congregation.
Kehillah: a community. And the verb, to gather people together. First, the great gathering.
Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses gives an instruction for the festival of booths, once every seven years: read the teaching aloud to everyone.
Look who's on the list: "Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that is within thy gates."
Not the leaders, not the scholars: the whole crowd, kids and newcomer included, so that, the verse says, they may hear and learn. The rabbis called this gathering hakhel: gather.

teach.h: KEHILLAH: THE COMMUNITY THAT SHOWS UP.
teach.b: Second, the community that lasts. For centuries, a Jewish town's organized community, with its synagogue, its burial society, its charity fund, its school, was called a kehillah.
It's the people who show up for a wedding, a shiva house, a bris, a sick neighbor. Some congregations still use the word in their names. Third, the warning.
In the sayings of the fathers, Hillel teaches: don't separate yourself from the community. Hillel's word there is a different one, tzibbur, but the point lands on kehillah.
You can learn alone, and pray alone, but the tradition keeps pulling you back toward the room full of other people.
Even Kohelet, with his big questions, takes his name from the crowd he spoke them to.

how: Jewish communities are often called kehillot, and Jewish life gathers people for prayer, learning and the life cycle; some communities hold a hakhel gathering in the year after the sabbatical year, recalling Deuteronomy 31.

games.q: it's been a hard year with your congregation, and you're tempted to go it alone. what does Hillel teach?
o: don't separate yourself from the community.
start a new group of people who agree with you.
games.why: in the sayings of the fathers, Hillel says: don't separate yourself from the community. the tradition keeps pulling you back toward the room.

practice: Let your circles come to mind as rooms full of faces: family, friends, coworkers, a class, a street, a congregation, and notice one that hasn't gathered in a while.
Picture them at one table, then add someone usually left off the list, the newcomer, the stranger within your gates. If you pray, you can hold that circle in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: K-H-L. Kuf, hey, lamed: the root of kahal, the assembly; kehillah, the community; hakhel, the great gathering; and Kohelet, the Gatherer. Today's word.
